objectives: Say who Ahmed Yesevî was.
Explain what Sufis try to do.
Explain the words hikmet and pîr.
Use is called and means.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter introduces Ahmed Yesevî and two key words: hikmet and pîr. A word card (word → meaning → example) helps learners keep the new words.
anticipatedMisconceptions: ‘Hikmet’ is the name of his poems; ‘pîr’ is a title for him.
Ahmed Yesevî started a Sufi school; he was not a king.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: is / are called · means · was the first … to
Look (Activity 1): His poems are called ‘hikmet’.
Practise (Activity 2): fill called and means.
Likely errors: *His poems call · *The word mean.
Use (Activity 3): names and meanings.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ah-MED ye-se-VÎ, PÎR-i tur-kis-TAN, hik-MET.
Stress: WIS-dom, SU-fi.
beforeReading: Ask: “Who was a wise teacher in your life?”
duringReading: First reading: Who was Ahmed Yesevî?
Second reading: make two word cards: hikmet and pîr.
Find what Sufis try to do.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Word cards; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: names and meanings; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why was Ahmed Yesevî important?
What did his school want to teach?
What does a guide do?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Hikmet” and “Pîr-i Turkistan” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: Sufi poet, wisdom, close to, behave well, guide, find peace.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the word cards with the words written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about Ahmed Yesevî with is called and means.

expectedResponses: Ahmed Yesevî was the first great Sufi poet to write in Turkish. His poems are called ‘hikmet’. He is also called Pîr-i Turkistan.
content.transferTask: Write about a name you know.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the two key words?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “is called” about Ahmed Yesevî.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners say three sentences about Ahmed Yesevî. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads up to “behave well” and B reads the rest. Each tells the partner two facts without looking. The partner writes them down, then both check in the text.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Groups of three. Reader reads the sentences about Sufis. Asker asks “How do Sufis live?” Checker checks the answer in the text.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “Who was Ahmed Yesevî?” The learner answers in three short sentences and says what “pîr” means.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Ahmed Yesevî was the first great Sufi poet to write in Turkish.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, who Ahmed Yesevî was and what his poems are called. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Ahmed Yesevî has a second name. What is it, and why does he have it?” (Pîr-i Turkistan, because he was a guide for people.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name the poems (hikmet), the school and the meaning of “pîr”.

thinkAloud.strategy: Guess a word from its sentence
thinkAloud.sentence: The Persian word ‘pîr’ means an elder or a guide.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The word “means” tells me the next words explain “pîr”. So I do not need a dictionary here. A pîr is an elder or a guide. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Sufis try to be very close to Allah.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What do Sufis try to do?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Who is a wise teacher in your life?
onlineTask.reply: Ask your classmate one question about his or her teacher.

objectives: Describe Ahmed Yesevî’s life in order.
Name the places where he lived and studied.
Say who his teachers were.
Use when, after and then.
content.pedagogy: A life story with several places. A simple map route (East Turkestan → Yesi → Bukhara → Yesi) helps learners follow the chapter. Modern country names in the text connect the old places with today.
priorKnowledge: Past simple of regular and irregular verbs.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Yesi is in Kazakhstan today; Bukhara is in Uzbekistan today.
He returned to Yesi at the end of his life; he did not stay in Bukhara.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: when + past · after + clause · then · until
Look (Activity 1): When he was young, he moved …
Practise (Activity 2): choose When, After and Then.
Likely errors: *When he young · *After his masters die.
Use (Activity 3): my life story.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: YE-si, bu-KHA-ra, AR-slan BA-ba, ka-zakh-STAN, uz-BEK-i-stan.
Stress: ed-u-CA-tion, RE-gion.
beforeReading: Ask: “Where were you born? Where do you live now?”
duringReading: First reading: Where did Ahmed Yesevî live?
Second reading: draw his route on a simple map.
Find his teachers.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–18 Map route; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: my life story; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did he go to Bukhara?
What was Turkestan like at that time?
Where did he spend the end of his life?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Yesi” and “Bukhara” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: wise, masters, death.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the map with the four places marked.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write Ahmed Yesevî’s life in five sentences with when, after and then.

expectedResponses: When he was young, Ahmed Yesevî moved to Yesi and studied with Arslan Baba. After Arslan Baba’s death, he traveled to Bukhara. Then, he returned to Yesi and guided people until 1166.
content.transferTask: Write about your life with when, after and then.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners follow the route on the map?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “when” and one with “after” about Ahmed Yesevî.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners tell a partner the places in Ahmed Yesevî’s life in the right order. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraph 2. Each tells the partner three facts. Together they draw his journey on a map.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentences about Bukhara. Asker asks “Where is Bukhara today?” Checker finds the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A tourist in Kazakhstan asks, “Why is the city of Yesi famous?” The learner answers in two sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Then, he returned to Yesi and guided people there until he died in 1166.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, where Ahmed Yesevî grew up and studied. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer says where these cities are today. Why?” (So readers can find them on a modern map.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The places are in the right order: East Turkestan, Yesi, Bukhara, Yesi. Learners use “then” or “after”.

thinkAloud.sentence: Some time after Arslan Baba’s death, he traveled to Bukhara.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “After” tells me the order. First Arslan Baba died, then Ahmed Yesevî went to Bukhara. I put Bukhara after Yesi on my map. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Ahmed Yesevî studied with Arslan Baba, a wise teacher, and got a good education.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Who was his first teacher?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Which city in your country is a center for education?
onlineTask.reply: Ask your classmate why he or she chose that city.

objectives: Say where Ahmed Yesevî became famous.
Explain why people loved him.
Use because and so.
content.pedagogy: A very short chapter with one clear reason: simple language and words of wisdom. It ends with a question that leads into the next chapter: What is wisdom?
anticipatedMisconceptions: People loved him for his simple language, not for money or power.
The chapter ends with a question; the answer comes in Chapter 4.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: because (reason) · so (result)
Look (Activity 1): … because he used simple language.
Practise (Activity 2): choose because or so.
Likely errors: *because of he used · *so because.
Use (Activity 3): a good speaker.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: tash-KENT, SYR DAR-ya.
Linking: “won the hearts” /wʌn ðə hɑːrts/.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do you like a teacher who uses simple words? Why?”
duringReading: First reading: Where did he become famous?
Second reading: underline the reason with because.
Find the question at the end.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–9 First reading; 9–14 Reason and result; 14–18 Quick Challenge; 18–30 Language Focus 1–2; 30–37 Use: a good speaker; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did people love Ahmed Yesevî?
Why is simple language important for a teacher?
What do you think wisdom is?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Tashkent” and “The Syr Darya River” when the picture is in place.
This chapter has no Word Notes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the sentence frame: People loved him because …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about a good teacher with because and so.

expectedResponses: Ahmed Yesevî became famous near Tashkent and along the Syr Darya River. People loved him because he used simple language and spoke words of wisdom.
content.transferTask: Talk about a person who speaks well.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners link simple language with winning hearts?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “because” about Ahmed Yesevî.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why people loved Ahmed Yesevî. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner reads the chapter and tells a partner why people loved Ahmed Yesevî. The partner says it in one sentence with “because”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the last sentence. Asker asks “What is the question?” Checker says which chapter answers it.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A friend asks, “How can a teacher win the hearts of students?” The learner answers and uses Ahmed Yesevî as an example.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “He won the hearts of the people because he used simple language and spoke words of wisdom (hikmet).” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why the Turkic people loved Ahmed Yesevî. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the chapter end with a question?” (It makes the reader want to read the next chapter.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give two reasons with “because”. They name Tashkent or the Syr Darya River.

thinkAloud.sentence: He won the hearts of the people because he used simple language and spoke words of wisdom (hikmet).
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Won the hearts” cannot mean a game here. It means people loved him. “Because” gives me the reason: simple language and wise words. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “During this time, he became famous among the Turkic people near Tashkent and along the Syr Darya River.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Where did he become famous?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Why is simple language important for a teacher?
onlineTask.reply: Give your classmate one more reason.

objectives: Explain what wisdom is in simple words.
Say which questions rules and wisdom answer.
Explain why the question ‘Why?’ is the most important.
Use without, but, only … when and because of.
content.pedagogy: An idea chapter with no story. A three-question chart (What? How? Why?) makes the abstract idea concrete: rules tell us what and how, wisdom tells us why.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Wisdom does not replace rules; it gives them a reason and a purpose.
“Empty tasks” means jobs done without meaning, not jobs that are easy.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: without + noun · but · only … when · because of + noun
Look (Activity 1): Without it, rules … are just empty tasks.
Practise (Activity 2): choose but, when and of.
Likely errors: *without of it · *because wisdom (no of).
Use (Activity 3): why do we do it?
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: PUR-pose, DU-ties, WIS-dom.
Intonation: What? How? Why? (rising, then falling).
duringReading: First reading: What is wisdom?
Second reading: complete the chart: What? How? Why?
Find the most important question.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Question chart; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: why do we do it?; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What are “empty tasks”?
Why is ‘Why?’ the most important question?
When do our actions have real meaning?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Why?” and “What? How?” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: reason, purpose, duties, empty tasks, rules, meaning.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with “What?” filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about a school rule and its purpose.

expectedResponses: Rules answer the questions ‘What?’ and ‘How?’, but wisdom answers the question ‘Why?’. Without wisdom, duties are just empty tasks.
content.transferTask: Explain why a rule at home or at school is important.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect wisdom with purpose?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “without” and one with “but”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain the difference between rules and wisdom. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 2 and explains which questions law and wisdom answer. B gives an example from school life.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 3. Asker asks “When do our actions have a real meaning?” Checker finds the sentence.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A younger student asks, “Why do we have to do homework?” The learner answers the “Why?” question, not only the “What?”.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Our actions only have a real meaning when we know the purpose.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what wisdom (hikmet) is and why the question “Why?” is important. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What happens to rules without wisdom, according to the chapter?” (They are just empty tasks.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners match law and rules with “What?” and “How?”, and wisdom with “Why?”.

thinkAloud.sentence: Wisdom helps us understand the reason and purpose of our actions.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: This is the first sentence, and the rest of the chapter explains it. So it is the main idea. I can say the whole chapter in this one sentence. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Without it, rules and duties are just empty tasks.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What are rules and duties without wisdom?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Choose one school rule and explain why we have it.
onlineTask.reply: Tell your classmate if you agree with his or her reason.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: The Child Who Respected the Qur’an
objectives: Retell the story of the child who respected the Qur’an.
Explain the two ways the child showed respect.
Explain why Ahmed Yesevî invited the child.
Use the past continuous with the past simple.
content.pedagogy: A short, memorable story about respect for the Qur’an and for a teacher. The child’s small actions show great respect, and Ahmed Yesevî notices them. The child later becomes Süleyman, the main person of the next chapters.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The child carried the Qur’an on his head to show respect, not because he had no bag.
He walked backwards so he did not turn his back to his teacher.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past continuous (was / were + -ing) · past simple for a short action · to + verb (purpose)
Look (Activity 1): Ahmed Yesevî was sitting … He saw …
Practise (Activity 2): fill were, were and was.
Likely errors: *They was going · *He was carry.
Use (Activity 3): showing respect.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: per-MIS-sion, BACK-wards, re-SPECT.
Names: sü-ley-MAN.
beforeReading: Ask: “How do people show respect to books in your home?”
duringReading: First reading: What did the child do?
Second reading: put four events in order.
Find the child’s name.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Story order; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: showing respect; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the child carry the Qur’an on his head?
Why did he walk backwards?
What did Ahmed Yesevî understand?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Qur’an on His Head” and “Walking Backwards” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: mosque, warm smile, turn his back, permission, became closer.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the four events on cards to order.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the story from the child’s point of view in five sentences.

formativeAssessment: Explains how the child showed respect.
expectedResponses: Ahmed Yesevî was sitting in front of his school. One child was carrying the Qur’an on his head to show respect, and he walked backwards on his way back. Yesevî invited him to his lessons.
content.transferTask: Write about how you show respect.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice the small actions that showed respect?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “was + -ing” about the story.

rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the third and fourth paragraphs.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners tell the story of the child who respected the Qur’an in four steps. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 3 and B reads paragraph 4. Each retells the part with books closed. The partner asks one “Why?” question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about walking backwards. Asker asks “Why did the child walk backwards?” Checker reads the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A younger child asks, “How can I show respect to my teacher?” The learner gives two ideas from the story.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Ahmed Yesevî saw this and understood the beautiful meaning in the child’s behavior.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, the story of the boy who carried the Qur’an on his head. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The child shows respect two times. What are the two times?” (He carries the Qur’an on his head, and he walks backwards.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the events in order and say the child’s name at the end.

thinkAloud.sentence: He did not want to turn his back on his teacher.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: This sentence explains the sentence before it. The child walked backwards for a reason. He wanted to show respect. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “However, one child was carrying the Qur’an on top of his head to show great respect.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: How was this child different from the other children?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: How do people show respect to teachers in your culture?
onlineTask.reply: Ask your classmate one question about his or her answer.

objectives: Retell the story of the wood in the rain.
Explain how Süleyman showed love for his duty.
Explain why Ahmed Yesevî called him Hakîm Süleyman.
Use so, however and from now on.
content.pedagogy: A story about responsibility and thinking ahead. Süleyman thought about the purpose of the wood, so he protected it. The story links with Chapter 4: knowing the ‘why’ of a duty is wisdom.
priorKnowledge: Past simple of irregular verbs (took, knew, told).
anticipatedMisconceptions: Süleyman wrapped his coat around the wood, not around himself.
‘Hakîm’ means wise; it was a new name, not a job.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: so (result) · however (contrast) · from now on · phrasal verb take off
Look (Activity 1): However, Süleyman’s wood was dry.
Practise (Activity 2): choose so, However and From now on.
Likely errors: *however, (in the middle without a new sentence) · *took of.
Use (Activity 3): a job I do well.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: SÜ-ley-man, ha-KÎM, DER-vish-es, how-EV-er.
Sound: wood /wʊd/, wet /wet/.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do you do when it starts to rain and you have something important?”
duringReading: First reading: What happened to the wood?
Second reading: make a chart: other wood / Süleyman’s wood.
Find Süleyman’s new name.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: a job I do well; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the school need the wood?
Why did Süleyman keep the wood dry?
Why did Ahmed Yesevî call him wise?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Rain” and “Dry Wood” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: took off, wrapped, duty, respect.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with one word in each column.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Act out the story in three short scenes.

formativeAssessment: Explains why Süleyman was called wise.
expectedResponses: It started to rain, so Süleyman wrapped his coat around his wood. All the other wood was wet. However, his wood was dry, and Ahmed Yesevî called him Hakîm Süleyman.
content.transferTask: Write about a job you do carefully.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners link the story with the idea of wisdom in Chapter 4?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “so” and one with “However”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain how Süleyman got the name “Süleyman the Wise”. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner reads the chapter up to “wrapped it around his wood” and tells a partner. The partner reads the rest and tells the ending.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about the other wood. Asker asks “Why did the other wood not burn?” Checker finds the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A friend asks, “What does it mean to do a job with a wise heart?” The learner answers with the story of the wood.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Ahmed Yesevî saw the boy’s great respect and love for his duty.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Süleyman kept the wood dry and got a new name. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Süleyman thought about the purpose of his job. How does this link to the chapter about wisdom?” (He knew why they needed dry wood.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners use “so” and “because” in the retelling and give the new name.

thinkAloud.sentence: Süleyman knew that they needed dry wood to cook the food, so he wanted to keep it dry.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “So” shows a result. Süleyman knew the purpose of the wood. That is why he used his coat. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “On their way back, it started to rain.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What did the school need the wood for?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences about a time you thought about the purpose of a job.
onlineTask.reply: Tell your classmate what he or she did well.

objectives: Say what Süleyman did after his Sufi education.
Say where Khwarazm is today.
Compare Hakîm Ata with Ahmed Yesevî.
Use after + -ing and just like.
content.pedagogy: A short bridge chapter: the student grows up and becomes a teacher himself. The comparison “just like his master” shows how knowledge passes from teacher to student.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Hakîm Ata is the same person as Süleyman.
Khwarazm is in Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan today, not in Kazakhstan.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: after + -ing · just like · under someone’s guidance
Look (Activity 1): After finishing his Sufi education, …
Practise (Activity 2): choose After, Just like and under.
Likely errors: *After finish · *just same as.
Use (Activity 3): just like my teacher.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: KHWA-razm, ha-KÎM A-ta, turk-men-i-STAN.
Stress: GUID-ance, ed-u-CA-tion.
beforeReading: Ask: “What did you learn from an older person that you now teach others?”
duringReading: First reading: What did Süleyman do after his education?
Second reading: make a chart: Ahmed Yesevî / Hakîm Ata.
Find where Khwarazm is today.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Comparison chart; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: just like my teacher; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did people call him Hakîm Ata?
What did he do in Khwarazm?
How was he like his master?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Khwarazm” and “Poems in Turkish” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: education, region, poems.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with “wrote poems in Turkish” in both columns.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences comparing Hakîm Ata and Ahmed Yesevî.

formativeAssessment: Says what he did after his education.
expectedResponses: After finishing his Sufi education, Hakîm Ata moved to Khwarazm. There, he taught and guided people. Just like his master, he wrote poems in Turkish.
content.transferTask: Talk about how you are like a teacher or an older person.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see how knowledge passes from teacher to student?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “after + -ing” and one with “just like”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners say three sentences about Hakîm Ata’s life after school. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads up to “moved to Khwarazm” and B reads the rest. Each tells the partner two facts.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the last sentence. Asker asks “How was Hakîm Ata like his master?” Checker checks the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A tourist in Uzbekistan asks, “Who was Hakîm Ata?” The learner answers in three short sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “There, he taught and guided people.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, where Hakîm Ata went and what he did there. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Which words in this chapter show that Hakîm Ata became like his teacher?” (He taught, guided people and wrote poems in Turkish.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name Khwarazm and give one way Hakîm Ata was like Ahmed Yesevî.

thinkAloud.sentence: Just like his master Ahmed Yesevî, Hakîm Ata also wrote poems in Turkish.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Just like” and “also” show me that two people do the same thing. The student does what his master did. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Later, people knew him by the name Hakîm Ata.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: By what name did people know him later?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: What did you learn from a teacher that you can teach others?

objectives: Explain why Hakîm Ata is important for the Turks.
Explain his two famous sayings in simple English.
Explain what being humble means.
Use not as … as, one of the first and see … as.
content.pedagogy: The closing chapter gives Hakîm Ata’s famous words about hospitality and humility. Learners explain old wise words in simple modern English, then build a class wisdom wall from the whole book. The Turkish versions stay in brackets, as in the book.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Not as famous as” does not mean “not famous”; it means less famous than his teacher.
“Others are wheat, we are chaff” is about being humble; it does not mean that he was a bad person.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: not as … as · one of the first + plural noun · see … as (imperative)
Look (Activity 1): not as famous as his teacher.
Practise (Activity 2): choose as, people and as.
Likely errors: *not as famous than · *one of the first person.
Use (Activity 3): welcoming a guest.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: KHI-zr, LAY-lat al-QADR.
Stress: HUM-ble, VIS-i-tor.
beforeReading: Ask: “What does it mean to be humble?”
duringReading: First reading: Why is Hakîm Ata important?
Second reading: explain each saying in simple English.
Find the words about being humble.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–17 Explain the sayings; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: welcoming a guest; 38–40 Exit ticket. (Wisdom wall in a second lesson.)
discussionPoints: How did Hakîm Ata help the Turks?
What does “see every visitor as Khizr” teach us?
Why does he say “we are chaff”?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Every Visitor” and “Being Humble” when the picture is in place.
The group task “Our Wisdom Wall” closes the book.
This chapter has no Word Notes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give sentence frames: This means that …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short dialogue: a family welcomes a guest and remembers Hakîm Ata’s words.

formativeAssessment: Explains why Hakîm Ata is important.
expectedResponses: Hakîm Ata is not as famous as his teacher, but he is one of the first people to teach Islam and good manners to the Turks. His words teach us to welcome every visitor and to be humble.
content.transferTask: Write about how your family welcomes guests.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners explain the sayings in their own words?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “not as … as”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain one of Hakîm Ata’s sayings in your own words. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A explains the saying about visitors and B explains the saying about wheat. Each partner asks “What does it mean for us today?”
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads one saying. Asker asks “What does this saying teach?” Checker finds the word “humble” in the text.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A guest comes to your home. A family member asks, “Why are you so kind to every guest?” The learner answers with Hakîm Ata’s words.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “He also has beautiful words about being humble: “Others are wheat, we are chaff; others are good, we are bad.”” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, one saying of Hakîm Ata and what it teaches. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does Hakîm Ata compare people to wheat and chaff?” (Wheat is useful and chaff is not. He shows that we should be humble.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain one saying in simple words and use “humble”.

thinkAloud.sentence: He also has beautiful words about being humble: “Others are wheat, we are chaff; others are good, we are bad.”
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: Wheat is useful, but chaff is not. The writer tells me first that the words are about being humble. So the saying means: do not think you are better than others. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “But he is one of the first people to teach Islam and good manners to the Turks.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What did Hakîm Ata teach the Turks?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Which saying from your family do you like?
onlineTask.reply: Tell your classmate what his or her saying means to you.

metadata.title: Ahmed Yesevî A2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Hoca Ahmed Yesevî and His Student Süleyman the Wise (Ahmed Yesevî)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 8 chapter units of 40 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Young learners and adults who can read short, simple texts about people, places and values, and who can write short connected sentences.
metadata.purpose: Develop A2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through Ahmed Yesevî and his student Hakîm Ata: a wise teacher, the meaning of wisdom and two stories about respect and duty, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned in small steps: in the Language Focus, learners first LOOK at a form in a real chapter sentence, then PRACTISE it in controlled, meaningful tasks, and finally USE it in short YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 8 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Look → Practise → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a picture or a word from daily life.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: a life in order, an idea with questions or a story in order.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (look → practise → use), then a short production about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Text-based and in small steps. Start from the story sentence, ask a simple meaning question (What does this word show?), let learners answer, then confirm the rule and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: is / are called · means · was the first … to
Ch2: when + past · after + clause · then · until
Ch4: without + noun · but · only … when · because of + noun
Ch5: past continuous (was / were + -ing) · past simple for a short action · to + verb (purpose)
Ch6: so (result) · however (contrast) · from now on · phrasal verb take off
Ch7: after + -ing · just like · under someone’s guidance
Ch8: not as … as · one of the first + plural noun · see … as (imperative)

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, people and key events.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: find key information, put events in order and understand simple reasons.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe people, rules and good actions in short connected sentences.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: write short connected sentences with and, but, so and because.

valuesFocus: D14 Respect — Respect for the Qur’an, for teachers and for elders.
D16 Responsibility — Doing a duty with care.
D20 Helpfulness — Welcoming guests and helping others.
D3 Diligence — Learning patiently from a teacher.
languageFocus: Every one of the 8 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Look → Practise → Use (3 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, picture cards, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.
The stories about Ahmed Yesevî and Süleyman are told in the book as famous stories; read them as they are.
Hakîm Ata’s sayings and the bracketed Turkish words belong to the teacher-approved text; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: Ahmed Yesevî and Hakîm Ata link Central Asia with questions every community faces today: how to teach with simple words, how to do a duty with care and how to welcome guests.

themes.title: Simple words, big ideas:
themes.description: Ahmed Yesevî won hearts with simple language (Chapter 3). Discuss why clear words help people understand each other.

themes.title: Knowing the why:
themes.description: Wisdom answers the question ‘Why?’ (Chapter 4). Discuss the purpose of rules at school and in society.

themes.title: Welcoming guests:
themes.description: Hakîm Ata asks us to see every visitor as Khizr (Chapter 8). Discuss how people welcome guests in different cultures.

actions: Ask an older family member for a wise saying and write it down.
Make a small poster: “Why do we follow this rule?”
Find Yesi, Bukhara and Khwarazm on a modern map.

exitTicket: One thing I learned about Ahmed Yesevî or Süleyman today is …
One new word from today’s chapter is …
One good action I can do this week is …

miniProject.title: Our Wisdom Wall
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose three wise sentences from the book, write each on a card with a small picture and one sentence that explains it, and put them on the class wall.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Wise Person I Know
reflectivePrompt.desc: Ahmed Yesevî called Süleyman wise because he thought about the purpose of his duty (Chapter 6). Write four to five sentences about a wise person you know. What does this person do or say?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect: The child carried the Qur’an on his head and did not turn his back to his teacher (Chapter 5).

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility: Süleyman kept the wood dry because he knew the school needed it to cook food (Chapter 6).

items.label: D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Helpfulness: The wood was for the dervishes, students and guests, and Hakîm Ata asks us to see every visitor as Khizr (Chapters 6 and 8).

items.label: D3 Diligence
items.value: Diligence: Ahmed Yesevî traveled to learn from great teachers, and Süleyman studied for many years (Chapters 2 and 5).

questions: What small action can show it this week?
Which part is from the book and which part is my own idea?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR A2. The table links the A2 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test A2 to the chapters of this book where learners practice them.

rows.descriptor: Can understand short, simple texts containing the highest frequency vocabulary, including a proportion of shared international vocabulary items.
practice: Chapter 5 (The Child Who Respected the Qur’an): Put the events of the story in order.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write a series of simple phrases and sentences linked with simple connectors like “and”, “but” and “because”.
practice: Chapter 6 (Wood in the Rain): Write three sentences about a job you do carefully.
Language Review, “Use: A Wise Person I Know”: Write four to five sentences.

rows.descriptor: Can give a simple description or presentation of people, living or working conditions, daily routines, likes/dislikes, etc. as a short series of simple phrases and sentences linked into a list.
practice: Chapter 3 (Words That Won Hearts): Talk about a person who speaks well.
Chapter 8 (Words of Hakîm Ata): Explain one card on the class wisdom wall.

test.title: End-of-Level Test A2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the A2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 60 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (40 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (20 minutes): on paper. Write an email to a friend about a visit to an old place. (50–70 words)
Speaking (about 6 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

Draw his route on a map.

Write one sentence with guided.

selfCheck: Can I explain wisdom?

mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, how Süleyman kept the wood dry and got a new name.

thinkAloud.sentence: Süleyman knew that they needed dry wood to cook the food, so he wanted to keep it dry.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “So” shows a result. Süleyman knew the purpose of the wood. That is why he used his coat. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “On their way back, it started to rain.”
stopAndCheck.question: What did the school need the wood for? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can say what Süleyman did after his Sufi education.
I can compare Hakîm Ata with his master.
I can use after + -ing and just like.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “After finishing his Sufi education”: the first action. Then choose After, Just like and under.
content.lessonPlan: What did you learn from an older person? Write one thing. Read the chapter and find where Hakîm Ata moved. Make a chart: Ahmed Yesevî, Hakîm Ata.
discussionPoints: Hakîm Ata learned from his teacher and then taught others. What can you teach a younger person this week?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Khwarazm” and “Poems in Turkish” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the second sentence again. Find “by the name”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Tell your partner how you are like an older person.

whatToNotice: The student became a teacher himself.
He wrote poems in Turkish like his master.
readListen: What did you learn from an older person? Write one thing.
Read the chapter and find where Hakîm Ata moved.
Make a chart: Ahmed Yesevî, Hakîm Ata.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: education, region, poems.
“He grew up under his guidance.” What is guidance?
Write one sentence with taught.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose his later name. Read the second sentence.
selfCheck: Can I say what he did?
Can I compare him with his master?
Can I use after + -ing?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Tell your partner how you are like an older person.
content.reflectionPrompt: Hakîm Ata learned from his teacher and then taught others. What can you teach a younger person this week?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Say three sentences about Hakîm Ata’s life after school. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “There, he taught and guided people.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, where Hakîm Ata went and what he did there.

thinkAloud.sentence: Just like his master Ahmed Yesevî, Hakîm Ata also wrote poems in Turkish.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “Just like” and “also” show me that two people do the same thing. The student does what his master did. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “Later, people knew him by the name Hakîm Ata.”
stopAndCheck.question: By what name did people know him later? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can explain why Hakîm Ata is important.
I can explain his famous words in simple English.
I can use not as … as and one of the first.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “not as famous as his teacher”: Ahmed Yesevî is more famous. Then choose as, people and as.
content.lessonPlan: What does it mean to be humble? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find why Hakîm Ata is important. Explain each saying in simple English.
discussionPoints: Hakîm Ata says: see every visitor as Khizr. How can you welcome a guest or a new friend well this week?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Every Visitor” and “Being Humble” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the first sentence again. Find “not as famous as”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write three sentences about how your family welcomes guests.

whatToNotice: Hakîm Ata taught the Turks with wise words.
His words are about guests and being humble.
readListen: What does it mean to be humble? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find why Hakîm Ata is important.
Explain each saying in simple English.
findAnswerInStory: Find how we should see every visitor.
Find the words about wheat and chaff.
vocabularyInContext: This chapter has no Word Notes.
“Being humble.” What does humble mean?
Write one sentence with visitor.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will decide if a statement is true or false. Read the first sentence.
selfCheck: Can I explain why he is important?
Can I explain a saying?
Can I use not as … as?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write three sentences about how your family welcomes guests.
content.reflectionPrompt: Hakîm Ata says: see every visitor as Khizr. How can you welcome a guest or a new friend well this week?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain one of Hakîm Ata’s sayings in your own words. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “He also has beautiful words about being humble: “Others are wheat, we are chaff; others are good, we are bad.”” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, one saying of Hakîm Ata and what it teaches.

thinkAloud.sentence: He also has beautiful words about being humble: “Others are wheat, we are chaff; others are good, we are bad.”
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: Wheat is useful, but chaff is not. The writer tells me first that the words are about being humble. So the saying means: do not think you are better than others. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “But he is one of the first people to teach Islam and good manners to the Turks.”
stopAndCheck.question: What did Hakîm Ata teach the Turks? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

metadata.title: Ahmed Yesevî A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who read about Ahmed Yesevî and Hakîm Ata alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 8 chapters of Ahmed Yesevî.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Understand who Ahmed Yesevî was and what wisdom means.
Retell two stories about Süleyman and explain why he was called wise.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 8.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One thing about Ahmed Yesevî or Süleyman that I liked:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 8 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 3 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows respect, responsibility, helpfulness and diligence. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Respect: Respect: The child carried the Qur’an on his head and did not turn his back to his teacher (Chapter 5).
Responsibility: Responsibility: Süleyman kept the wood dry because he knew the school needed it to cook food (Chapter 6).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: The wood was for the dervishes, students and guests, and Hakîm Ata asks us to see every visitor as Khizr (Chapters 6 and 8).
Diligence: Diligence: Ahmed Yesevî traveled to learn from great teachers, and Süleyman studied for many years (Chapters 2 and 5).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 8, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell the story of the wood in the rain to someone at home in four sentences, in your home language or in English.
